messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The spill happened on a Tuesday afternoon in the banquet kitchen of the hotel where Anh had worked for twenty-three years. A junior line cook, rushing to prep for a wedding reception, knocked a five-gallon container of industrial degreaser off a high shelf. The chemical splashed across the hot range and vaporized instantly into a pale, acrid cloud. Anh was the first manager through the swinging doors. He shouted for everyone to evacuate, but by the time he turned to run, he had already taken three deep breaths of the air that now tasted like burnt metal and chlorine. For weeks afterward, even after the hotel’s ventilation was scrubbed and certified safe, Anh would walk into the banquet kitchen and taste that same chemical burn at the back of his throat. It would arrive without warning—while he was reviewing a staffing schedule, or standing in the grocery store aisle, or lying in bed next to his partner at three in the morning. The memory would not simply return to him. It would seize him. His chest would lock, his hands would begin to shake, and for a few terrible seconds he was back in that doorway, the cloud rolling toward him, certain that this was the moment his body would finally give out.

In the months that followed, Anh began to treat his own body as though it were a building with faulty wiring. He checked it constantly. Several times an hour, he would pause whatever he was doing and scan himself: his breathing, his pulse, the sensation in his lungs. A slight tightness in his chest that he would have ignored before now sent him into a spiral of focused attention. He would press his hand to his ribs, counting breaths, trying to decide whether this was normal fatigue or the first sign of something catastrophic. At work, he found himself scanning the environment with the same vigilance. Every hallway he walked, every storage closet he passed, every corner of the lobby—he checked for anything unusual: a strange smell, a misplaced container, a door left ajar. He told himself this was just being careful, that a good manager notices details. But the scanning never stopped, and it never made him feel safer. It only confirmed that danger was everywhere, waiting.

His body remained in a state of constant readiness. His shoulders were perpetually raised, his jaw tight, his stomach knotted. When a vendor was late with a linen delivery, Anh’s first thought was not that traffic was bad, but that something had happened—an accident, a chemical leak, a collapse. The delay itself felt like evidence of disaster. His partner noticed that he no longer sat through an entire meal without getting up to check the front door or the stove. He had begun to react to small, ordinary events as though they were alarms. A dropped tray in the kitchen would make him flinch so hard he would nearly knock his chair over. A sudden cough from a guest in the lobby would send a jolt through him. He knew, intellectually, that these things meant nothing. But knowing did not stop the reaction.

Anh had come to believe something more fundamental had broken. He could no longer trust his own body to keep him safe. It had betrayed him once, in that kitchen, and he was certain it would betray him again. He felt, at a level deeper than thought, that he no longer belonged anywhere—not in his hotel, where the smell of cleaning products now made his stomach turn, and not in his own life, which had become a series of precautions that never seemed to be enough. He avoided conversations about the incident. When a colleague mentioned it in passing, Anh would go silent, his face still, his mind racing. He stopped attending the monthly staff meetings where the safety protocols were reviewed. He told his partner he was just tired. But what he really felt was helpless: that no amount of checking or scanning or bracing would stop the next bad thing from happening.

What finally brought Anh to seek help was not the fear itself, but the exhaustion. He had spent six months on high alert, and his body could no longer sustain it. He had missed two important vendor negotiations because he could not bring himself to walk past the banquet kitchen. His general manager had pulled him aside and asked, with concern, whether everything was all right. Anh had said yes. But that night, lying awake, tasting metal in his mouth, he realized he was not all right. He was waiting for the next disaster. He was not sure he could survive it. And for the first time, he was almost willing to ask for help—if only he could believe that help would make any difference.
